newsitem.title: USA: U.S. weighs options to settle meat row with EU.
newsitem.headline: U.S. weighs options to settle meat row with EU.

text.p: With a self-imposed deadline closing in by which Washington has said it would take action to halt up to $300 million worth of meat shipments from Europe, U.S. officials searched Monday for a way out.

U.S. industry sources anticipated that Washington would avert a potentially nasty trade war with the European Union by agreeing to accept a deal in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks on everthing except poultry.

But sources cautioned that no final decisions had been made yet. "Things are not set in cement ... A lot of discussions are still taking place between the industry and USDA," said an industry official.
U.S. and EU officials ended face-to-face talks last Friday after failing to reach an agreement over meat import inspection regulations.

Officials kept in contact this past weekend through faxes and phone calls, and Washington was expected to announce on Tuesday whether it would go ahead with actions on April 15 to remove over 100 European meat and poulty plants from its list of approved exporters, or whether a deal had been worked out.
At day's end, it was confirmed that EU negotiators were coming back to Washington on Wednesday, and speculation was that they would discuss the unresolved poultry issues.
The complicated talks have covered a wide range of issues and sectors -- including the beef and pork industry, the poultry industry, the pet food sector, and the dairy and egg sectors.

Progress has apparently been made in several areas, but a bitter dispute over the decontamination method used by the U.S. poultry industry has turned out to be the key remaining obstacle towards finally settling the years-old dispute.

For that reason, U.S. officials were said to be considering separating poultry from the agreement and were reportedly looking at other options -- including taking the poultry issue to the World Trade Organisation -- to resolve that sticking point.

If the decision to exclude poultry is made, that would mean that U.S. poultry shipments to Europe -- which have been halted since April 1 due to new EU regulations -- would continue to be blocked. Some $50 million worth U.S. poultry is exported every year to the EU.

U.S. officials briefed poultry and red meat industry representatives Monday afternoon in separate sessions on what options they were looking at. Poultry industry officials said they would not be pleased if Washington reachs an agreement that does not include poultry.
"It would be an unfortunate situation. The poultry industry would not support this," said Bill Roenigk, senior vice president of the National Broiler Council.
But Roenigk noted that in the scope of the $3 billion worth of agricultural trade between Europe and the United States, $50 million may not seem like much.
"If you are in USDA's shoes and looking at $1.5 billion of agriculture being traded each way, it's a very difficult situation," said Roenigk.

Other meat industry officials said progress in other areas -- such as changing the way the EU approves U.S. meat and poultry plants for export -- could open Euorpean markets and was too important to throw away for a single issue.
